explain.say: See the first box? It really happened: a dog chased a cat up a tree. Now look at details drop. The next person forgets the tree. Psychologists call this levelling: small details fall away so the story gets shorter. What details do you forget when you retell a film?

explain.say: See bits get bigger? The next person makes the exciting part bigger: a huge dog attacked the cat! This is called sharpening. We keep and stretch the dramatic bits because they are fun to tell. Have you ever made a story a bit more exciting?

faq.q: Why do stories change when they are passed along?
faq.a: Because each person remembers and retells it a little differently: details drop out, exciting bits grow, and the story bends to fit what people expect. Small changes add up.
asks: Why does the telephone game go wrong?

faq.a: Levelling is when small details drop out as a story is retold, so it becomes shorter and simpler. Allport and Postman described it in their 1947 study of rumours.
Sharpening is when the few details people keep get made bigger or more dramatic, because exciting bits are easier to remember and fun to tell.
asks: Tell me about bits get bigger

faq.a: Assimilation is when people change a story to fit what they already believe, expect or fear. That is how ordinary events can turn into scary or biased stories.
asks: Tell me about fits our ideas
How do our beliefs change stories?

faq.q: How can I get the true version of a story?
faq.a: Go back to the first source: ask the person who saw it, or find the original report, rather than trusting a story that has passed through many people.
asks: How do I check a story?

facts: Gordon Allport and Leo Postman described levelling, sharpening and assimilation in "The Psychology of Rumor" (1947).
In 1932, Frederic Bartlett found that British students retelling a Native American folk tale changed it to fit their own culture.
